title: On-Policy Self-Distillation without Any Supervision
hook: Self-distillation that finally deserves the name: no ground truth, no bigger teacher — just a model voting against itself and fixing where it was confidently wrong.
key_points: Existing on-policy self-distillation still leans on ground truth, environment feedback, or a larger teacher — so it isn't really self-supervised.
U-OPSD samples several rollouts, builds a pseudo-solution by majority vote under a self-consistency threshold, then distills on the completions that disagree.
Conditioning on the pseudo-solution targets exactly the places the model is confidently wrong, rather than reinforcing what it already gets right.
On AIME24/25, HMMT25, MATH500 and AMC23, it lifts Qwen3 non-thinking mode by 8.5% at 4B and 10.7% at 8B over the base model.
It beats supervised OPSD by 3.2% (4B) and 2.3% (8B) on average, and stays level with OPSD and slightly ahead of GRPO in thinking mode.
content_html: On-policy distillation trains a model on its own generations rather than a fixed dataset, which keeps the training distribution honest — but in practice it has always needed something from outside: ground-truth answers, an environment that scores rollouts, or a larger teacher to imitate. A team from UC San Diego argues you can drop all three.
extra_html:
Their method, U-OPSD, samples several rollouts for a prompt and takes a majority vote — gated by a self-consistency threshold — as a pseudo-solution. It then conditions the model's distribution on that pseudo-solution and distills the model onto the completions that disagreed, so the update lands precisely where the model was confidently wrong rather than reinforcing what it already had right.

The numbers hold up across five math reasoning benchmarks (AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25, MATH500, AMC23). In Qwen3 non-thinking mode, U-OPSD gains 8.5% at 4B and 10.7% at 8B over the base model, and beats supervised OPSD by 3.2% and 2.3% on average. In thinking mode it stays roughly level with OPSD while edging past GRPO. Li et al., August 2026; code is on GitHub.

related.title: Rethinking On-Policy Self-Distillation for Thinking Models
related.hook: Giving a model the answer as privileged context sounds like it should only help. For thinking models on long reasoning traces, it backfires — accuracy drops up to 17%, and this explains why.

related.title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization via Direct On-Policy Distillation
related.hook: RL post-training gets pricier as models scale, since it needs the strong model's own rollouts. Direct-OPD reuses a cheap RL run on a small model instead, transferring the direction RL moved it.

flashcards.prompt: How does U-OPSD get a training target without any ground truth?
flashcards.back_html: It samples multiple rollouts and takes a majority vote under a self-consistency threshold as a pseudo-solution, then distills the model on the completions that disagree with it.

flashcards.prompt: Why do the authors say prior on-policy self-distillation isn't truly 'self'?

choices.text: It still relies on external supervision — ground truth, environment feedback, or a larger teacher
It trains on off-policy data collected from other models
It requires a second copy of the model held in frozen form

flashcards.explanation_html: The paper's framing is that once you need labels or a bigger teacher, the signal comes from outside the model — U-OPSD replaces that with internal consistency.

flashcards.prompt: What kind of errors is U-OPSD designed to attack?
flashcards.back_html: Cases where the model is confidently wrong — conditioning on the pseudo-solution isolates the disagreeing completions, so training pressure lands where the model's own consensus contradicts it.
